bottlenecks.reading: What NVIDIA supplies that is scarce: complete rack-scale AI systems (GPU + CPU + NVLink + networking + software). The Q2 FY2027 10-Q says Vera Rubin began production shipments in Q3 FY2027, that NVIDIA is "currently experiencing certain supply constraints" and has entered significant commitments to secure inventory and capacity "for the next several years". Data Center revenue was $89.0B in Q2 FY2027 vs $41.1B a year earlier (+117%).

Who needs it and pays: the cloud/AI capex of the largest buyers keeps rising in their own filings: latest-quarter capex y/y MSFT +110% ($35.8B), GOOGL +100% ($44.9B), AMZN +68% ($54.2B), META +80% ($33.9B), ORCL +235% ($28.5B). NVIDIA Hyperscale revenue $48.7B (+102% y/y) and AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise $40.3B (+138% y/y): the non-hyperscale buyers grow faster. Capex quarters are not aligned (calendar Q2 for GOOGL/AMZN/MSFT, Q3 for META, Jun-Aug for ORCL); capex is the buyer budget, not NVIDIA revenue. New since the earlier attempt: Meta's Q3 2026 release (2026-10-21) reports quarterly capex including finance-lease principal of $34.91B, free cash flow of negative $2.12B, and narrows its 2026 capex outlook to $135-145B (from $130-145B); the capex of Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon for the September quarter is not yet reported (late October, after as_of).

Market direction (attributed study, search excerpt only): Dell'Oro (2026-08-18) projects worldwide data center capex above $3 trillion by 2030, with high-end AI accelerators the largest share and main growth driver; its 2030 outlook nearly doubled since its January 2026 forecast (higher hyperscale capex guidance, more power capacity, higher commodity/memory costs). Dell'Oro states growth depends on the sustainability of investment, power availability and supply chain. Part of the dollar growth is price (memory), not units.

Who adds competing capacity, custom silicon: Broadcom AI semiconductor revenue $16.7B in its quarter to 2026-08-02 (221% y/y, 54% q/q), guided to $21.7B next quarter (236% y/y); Marvell data center revenue $2.17B (+46% y/y) with custom acceleration expected in H2 FY2027. Custom accelerators grow faster than NVIDIA Data Center (+117%) from a base about one-fifth the size. Derived revenue-scale comparison (NOT an attributed market share; scopes differ: NVIDIA DC includes networking and systems, AMD DC includes server CPUs, Broadcom AI includes networking): NVIDIA DC / (NVIDIA DC + AMD DC + Broadcom AI) = 79% for the nearest quarters, against about 83% a year earlier (derived from the reported y/y rates; see the fd SHARE notes).

Merchant GPU rival: AMD Data Center segment $6.7B (+107% y/y, base depressed by the $800M MI308 charge in Q2 2025); AMD guides Q3 2026 revenue $13B +/- $300M (~41% y/y) and says Helios racks begin to ramp in H2 2026. AMD sells to the same labs/clouds; its share gain is a lever on NVIDIA pricing, not yet visible in NVIDIA gross margin (flat sequentially in Q2 FY2027 per the CFO commentary).

AI networking competition: Arista revenue +38% y/y at a 45% GAAP operating margin and Cisco +18% y/y (latest quarters); NVIDIA no longer discloses networking revenue separately under its new market-platform framework, so its networking share cannot be measured from its own numbers (gap).

How firm the demand is: revenue from remaining performance obligations of contracts longer than one year was only $3.2B at 2026-07-26 (39% due within 12 months) against $89.0B of quarterly Data Center revenue: the order book is not long-term contracted take-or-pay, and the CFO commentary mentions extended payment terms on large multi-quarter agreements with certain investment-grade customers. Demand can turn faster than the supply commitments NVIDIA has signed.

How far NVIDIA has committed upstream (primary, 10-Q Note 10): supply and capacity commitments rose from $119 billion at the prior quarter to $279 billion at 2026-07-26 (of $366 billion total commitments; $92B falls in the rest of fiscal 2027, $87B in FY2028, $88B in FY2029), described as "primarily memory and manufacturing facilities" for long-term demand across current and future architectures; some agreements may be cancelable, rescheduled or adjustable before firm orders, with possible additional cost. NVIDIA also records $2.1B of excess-inventory purchase obligations as an accrued liability. The commitment is a fixed claim against a demand that is only short-cycle contracted (see fd_b_short_cycle_demand).

Upstream foundry reading (press report of the call, TSMC release and transcript not read): on 2026-10-15 TSMC's chairman and CEO said AI-related demand remained far above what TSMC can currently supply and that it is working to narrow the gap; TSMC reported September-quarter revenue of $46.72B (+41.2% y/y), HPC at 68% of revenue, guided the December quarter to $52.3-54.3B, expects about 44% full-year 2026 growth in USD, kept its 2026 capital budget at $60-64B, and said 2026-2028 capex will be significantly higher than the previous three years. No CoWoS capacity figure or end date was given in the report. This fits NVIDIA's own wording of current supply constraints, but it is one supplier's statement about all AI customers, not NVIDIA-specific.

Upstream bottleneck and its duration (secondary relays, not registered: publication dates not established): TSMC CoWoS advanced packaging and HBM memory limit how many accelerators anyone can ship. Relayed estimates put NVIDIA at about 60% of TSMC CoWoS capacity for 2026 (Morgan Stanley via TipRanks), Broadcom ~15% and AMD ~11%; CoWoS capacity estimates for end-2027 range widely (about 112k to 200k wafers/month); memory makers reportedly allocated all 2027 DRAM/HBM capacity (DigiTimes via TweakTown), with meaningful new memory capacity seen around 2028. If true, the shortage protects NVIDIA allocation and pricing into 2027 but raises its memory cost.

China (secondary relay, not registered): an IDC estimate relayed by press puts H1 2026 China data-center AI accelerator shares at NVIDIA 34% and Huawei 28% (NVIDIA units -44% y/y); Huawei Ascend 950PR in mass production since March 2026 and 960DT announced for Q1 2027. NVIDIA excludes China data center compute from its outlook (reports lane), so this is a lost-option reading, not a forecast driver.

fd SHARE (derived, scope-mismatched, NOT an attributed market share; revenue-scale comparison among the three named competitors that disclose AI/Data Center lines): NVIDIA Data Center revenue $89.0B in Q2 FY2027 (+117% y/y, so about $41.1B a year earlier, fd_s_nvda_cfo_q2fy27, pf_rel_20260826_1, pf_rel_20250827_1) against AMD Data Center segment $6.7B (+107% y/y, about $3.2B a year earlier, fd_s_amd_pr_q2_2026) and Broadcom AI semiconductors $16.7B (+221% y/y, about $5.2B a year earlier, fd_s_avgo_pr_q3fy26). NVIDIA share of the three: about 83.0% a year earlier, 79.2% now (-3.8 points); Broadcom 10.5% to 14.9% (+4.4 points); AMD 6.5% to 6.0% (-0.5 point). The three together grew about 127% y/y ($49.5B to $112.4B). Quarters are the nearest ones (NVIDIA to 2026-07-26, AMD to 2026-06-27, Broadcom to 2026-08-02); year-ago values are backed out of the reported growth rates, so they carry rounding of about +/-0.3 points. Broadcom AI includes networking and AMD Data Center includes server CPUs.

fd SHARE reading: on these numbers custom silicon (Broadcom, and in a smaller way Marvell) is taking relative share from NVIDIA, not the merchant GPU rival AMD; NVIDIA's absolute Data Center revenue still grew by about $48B y/y, so a share loss of about 4 points of this trio coincides with very fast growth for NVIDIA. Sequentially (nearest quarters) NVIDIA Data Center grew about 18% ($75.2B to $89.0B, pf_rel_20260520_1, pf_rel_20260826_1) against about 54% for Broadcom AI semiconductors (fd_s_avgo_pr_q3fy26), and Broadcom guides $21.7B next quarter (+30% q/q) while NVIDIA guides total revenue of $108B (+12% q/q, Data Center not guided separately, pf_rel_20260826_1). Marvell Data Center (+46% y/y) and Arista (+38% y/y) grow slower than NVIDIA Data Center (+117%) in the same quarters. Share of networking cannot be measured (NVIDIA no longer reports it).
